description: We are space enthusiasts from Ukraine building Shadowline, an interactive 3D navigator for lunar landing sites using NASA open data. We are strong in software development and DevOps and can build and deploy the whole product. We are looking for designers (UI/UX, infographics), data visualization and 3D fans, presenters to pitch our idea, writers, and video makers. No space background needed, just curiosity. Join us and bring light to lunar shadows!
summary:
Shadowline is a web app for choosing and comparing lunar landing sites and dates near the Moon’s south pole. For any point on the surface and any moment from November 2026 to October 2030, it computes where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the local terrain horizon. From that it derives solar power, battery charge, surface temperature and direct contact with NASA’s Deep Space Network. Everything runs in the browser, using preprocessed JPL DE440, LRO LOLA and Diviner data.

The site answers three questions: what light and contact does a spot have right now, where and when should a lander touch down, and what happens if the plan fails. The last one goes beyond the brief. Shadowline tests each plan against launch slip, landing miss, tip-over at touchdown and power loss after a tip-over, and its model was checked against the real SLIM, IM-1 and IM-2 landings.
This matters because near the pole the Sun skims the horizon. A few hundred metres or a few days can change power and communication by tens of percent, and recent landings show that a nominal plan is not enough.
details:
https://github.com/yevhensobol/Shadowline

Shadowline is a website for planning landing on Moon, with focus on souht pole. You click spot on map, pick date, and it tells you whether that spot wiil see Sun and Earth, how much power your panels will make, how cold it gets, and when you can talk to through DNS antennas in Goldstone, Madrid and Canberra.

The site itself is C# and Blazor running in the browser, so there’s no server and no login. It works in English and Uols for parts of the code and text, but every number comes from NASA data and our own calculations. Python scripts prepare epheremeris and terrain data in advance. Everything for pont and date you chose is computed in your browser. We used SI tools for parts of code. Values are computed by our code from cited Nasa and partner data, and few hand-entered inputs, such as lander parameters and mission event times, come from cited sources.

South pole is tricky. The Sun barely rises there, so tiny changes matter. Few hundred meters to the side, or a few days later, and a sunny site turns dark. To catch that, every point gets its own horizon from LOLA terrain data. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA’s SPICE toolkit.

What we cared about most was failure. Since 2023, six of nine landing attempts went wrong, and three landers fell over. So Shadowline also asks what happens if the launch slips, if you miss your target, or if you tip over. One result surprised us. For tripped lander like Athena, panels only on top deck give power in less than half of randomattitudes. Same panel area on its four sides give power in about 86%. We tested this on SLIM. From its January events alone, we estimated that its panels faced west, same JAXA reported. Our predicted window for power on next lunar day contains JAXA’s February contact, although simple "Sun is Up" rule also passes that check, so we read it as consistency, not proof.

At the Moon’s south pole, communication with Earth depends primarily on whether Earth is visible from landing site. Earth sits low on the horizon and wobbles due to libration, so ridges and crater walls regularly block it from view. Shadowline calculates, for every point and every moment, whether the Earth rises above the local horizon, taking into account the LOLA terrain data. As independent chek, our yerly sunlit share near pole was compared with LPLA team`s map (Mazarico et al.2011) correlation 0.985 mean difference about one percentage point.

The main communication tool taken into account in the project is the ground-based Deep Space Network. It is presented as a reference network comprising three complexes: Goldstone, Madrid and Canberra. These are positioned on a 3D model of the Earth, and a station is highlighted when it can see Moon at altitude of more than 10° above the horizon. Based on the calculations carried out, it can be said that at least one station can see the Moon 98 per cent of the time, with longest interruption lasting around 1.5 hours. In project, we are also drawing on the experience of past missions; IM-2: carried first LTE network on Moon with base station about 4 m above ground on lander. It powered on, but lander ended upon its side and no surface link was made. We use same geometry as LunarRF atlas: antenna on 4m mast and receiver 1.5m above ground, caried by rpver, hopper or astronait.

For any point south of 80° S, the LOLA terrain model with a resolution of 80 m is used to calculate which part of the surrounding area is directly visible. Result is shown for two radii: 2 km and 10 km. Separately, we calculate the visible area within a 22 km radius, i.e. the communication range at a frequency of 1.8 GHz. Location card and the report both include a 44 × 44 km map showing areas with direct line of sight and those obscured by terrain. This enables a better understanding of the situation and helps decide where to send the rover so that it does not lose communication. 

Engineer can work with report in one click turns any site into a full report: verdicts, time-series charts of Sun and Earth, power and battery, surface temperature, DSN contact, plan robustness, and a methods and sources section. It is built for the people who have to sign off on a landing, so every result comes in three levels: a plain verdict, the numbers behind it, and the method with references. The report can be printed to PDF, and also exported as JSON and CSV, so the same results can be read by a person, loaded into a spreadsheet or fed into a team’s own tools.

Report does not hide bad news. For each site it says plainly whether the plan holds if launch slips, if the lander misses by 100 m, 1 km or 5 km, if it tips over at touchdown, and whether the panels would still power the safe mode before the battery runs out. Our example report for IM-2 Athena shows “Not met” in red where the requirements fail, and gives the nearest start date that works. Real misses are shown beside each radius (SLIM 55 m, Apollo 12 164 m, IM-2 250 m), so a number like “1 km” has a meaning.

Up to three recommended zones can be placed side by side, each with its own robustness check, and the report adds a ground radio block: line of sight from a 4 m mast up to 22 km, checked against LunarRF. Every report is tied to a link that stores the site, time and mission settings, so a colleague opens exactly what you saw. All numbers are computed by scripts from NASA data, never typed in by hand or written by a language model.
